questions.q: What are the approximate physiological caloric (energy) yields per gram of carbohydrate, protein, and lipid (triacylglycerol) oxidized in the human body?
options: Carbohydrate ~4 kcal/g, protein ~4 kcal/g, lipid ~9 kcal/g
Carbohydrate ~9 kcal/g, protein ~4 kcal/g, lipid ~4 kcal/g
Carbohydrate ~4 kcal/g, protein ~9 kcal/g, lipid ~7 kcal/g
Carbohydrate ~2 kcal/g, protein ~4 kcal/g, lipid ~8 kcal/g
questions.explain: Complete oxidation yields roughly 4 kcal/g for digestible carbohydrates, ~4 kcal/g for dietary proteins (accounting for incomplete urea oxidation), ~9 kcal/g for triacylglycerols (due to higher carbon-hydrogen reduction state), and ~7 kcal/g for ethanol.

open.q: Approximately how many kilocalories per gram does dietary fat (triacylglycerol) yield upon oxidation?

questions.q: What does the respiratory quotient (RQ = CO2 produced / O2 consumed) indicate when a resting subject oxidizes primarily carbohydrate versus primarily long-chain fatty acids?
options: RQ is ~0.7 for carbohydrate and ~1.0 for fat
RQ is ~1.0 for carbohydrate and ~0.7 for fat
RQ is ~0.5 for carbohydrate and ~1.5 for fat
RQ is always 0.85 regardless of fuel source
questions.explain: Complete glucose oxidation (C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O) gives RQ = 6/6 = 1.0, whereas palmitate oxidation (C16H32O2 + 23 O2 -> 16 CO2 + 16 H2O) gives RQ = 16/23 ≈ 0.70; mixed diets yield RQ ≈ 0.82-0.85.

open.q: What is the theoretical respiratory quotient (RQ) for complete oxidation of glucose?

questions.q: How does kwashiorkor differ biochemically and clinically from marasmus in severe acute malnutrition?
options: Kwashiorkor features severe total calorie and fat/muscle wasting without edema, whereas marasmus causes hepatic steatosis and edema

Kwashiorkor presents with pitting edema, fatty liver (impaired VLDL export due to apolipoprotein synthesis deficit), skin/hair changes, and hypoalbuminemia despite relatively preserved subcutaneous fat compared with marasmus's extreme global wasting without edema
Marasmus is caused strictly by excess vitamin A
Kwashiorkor occurs only in adults with hyperthyroidism
questions.explain: In kwashiorkor, low plasma albumin reduces oncotic pressure causing edema, while impaired hepatic synthesis of apolipoprotein B-100 traps triacylglycerols in hepatocytes (steatosis); marasmus reflects chronic overall energy-protein deprivation with severe cachexia and minimal edema.

open.q: Which severe malnutrition syndrome is classically characterized by pitting edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hepatic steatosis?

questions.q: Which nine amino acids are nutritionally essential (indispensable) for adult humans because they cannot be synthesized endogenously at rates meeting physiological demand?
options: Alanine, aspartate, glutamate, glycine, serine, proline, arginine, cysteine, tyrosine
Histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine
Glutamine, asparagine, taurine, ornithine, citrulline, creatine, beta-alanine, GABA, hydroxyproline
Leucine, isoleucine, valine, alanine, glycine, proline, serine, cysteine, tyrosine
questions.explain: The nine indispensable amino acids in humans are histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine (PVT TIM HaLL); arginine is conditionally essential during growth, trauma, or urea cycle stress.

open.q: Name the three branched-chain essential amino acids.

questions.q: What is the biochemical basis of dietary protein complementation (such as combining legumes/beans with cereal grains like rice, maize, or wheat)?
options: Cereals are rich in lysine and poor in methionine, while legumes are rich in methionine and poor in lysine

Legumes (pulses) are rich in lysine but relatively limiting in sulfur amino acids (methionine/cysteine), whereas cereal grains are rich in methionine/cysteine but limiting in lysine, so eating them together supplies a balanced essential amino acid profile
Combining plant foods converts cellulose into glucose
Legumes supply vitamin B12 while grains supply vitamin D
questions.explain: Mutual amino acid complementation compensates for limiting amino acids in individual plant proteins, raising the biological value and net protein utilization of mixed plant meals.

open.q: Cereal grains are typically limiting in which essential amino acid that is abundant in legumes (beans/lentils)?

questions.q: How do soluble fermentable dietary fibers (such as beta-glucans, pectins, and inulin) exert metabolic benefits in the gastrointestinal tract?
options: Directly absorbed intact into arterial blood as high-energy monosaccharides

Form viscous gels that slow gastric emptying and glucose/bile acid absorption, while colonic microbiota ferment them into short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate) that nourish colonocytes (butyrate) and support metabolic/gut health
Inhibit all pancreatic amylase secretion permanently
Prevent all water absorption in the colon
questions.explain: Fermentable fibers yield short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): butyrate is the primary fuel for colonic epithelial cells and promotes anti-inflammatory regulatory T cells, propionate enters hepatic gluconeogenesis/lipid regulation, and binding bile acids promotes cholesterol clearance.

open.q: Name the short-chain fatty acid produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber that serves as the preferred energy source for colonocytes.

questions.q: Which visual pigment chromophore derived from all-trans-retinol (vitamin A) undergoes light-induced cis-to-trans isomerization in rod photoreceptors to initiate visual signal transduction?
options: 11-cis-retinal bound to opsin (forming rhodopsin)
Retinoic acid bound to RAR/RXR
Beta-carotene dimer
7-dehydrocholesterol
questions.explain: 11-cis-retinal is covalently attached via a Schiff base (protonated imine) to lysine-296 of opsin to form rhodopsin; absorption of a photon isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, activating transducin (Gt) and phosphodiesterase.

open.q: Name the cis-isomer of retinal that binds opsin to form rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors.

questions.q: Which active metabolite of vitamin A regulates gene transcription via nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR and RXR) to maintain epithelial differentiation and prevent squamous metaplasia?
options: 11-cis-retinol
Retinoic acid (all-trans-retinoic acid)
Cholecalciferol
Menaquinone
questions.explain: Retinoic acid acts as a steroid-like nuclear hormone ligand controlling epithelial cell differentiation and mucin synthesis; vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia, Bitot spots, night blindness, follicular hyperkeratosis, and immunosuppression.

open.q: Which vitamin A derivative acts primarily through nuclear receptors to regulate epithelial cell differentiation and gene expression?

questions.q: Why can excessive vitamin A intake or isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) during pregnancy cause severe fetal craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system malformations?
options: Retinoids alter homeobox (Hox) gene expression and neural crest cell migration/apoptosis during embryogenesis
Vitamin A depletes maternal folic acid in red blood cells
Retinoids block placental glucose transport
Vitamin A causes maternal rhabdomyolysis
questions.explain: Hypervitaminosis A and systemic retinoids during early pregnancy are potently teratogenic, disrupting morphogen gradients and neural crest patterning.

open.q: Is excess vitamin A (hypervitaminosis A) in early pregnancy teratogenic or non-teratogenic?

questions.q: Which sequential hydroxylations convert cutaneous cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) or dietary ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) into the active hormone calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3)?
options: First 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney, then 25-hydroxylation in the liver
First 25-hydroxylation in the liver (producing 25-hydroxyvitamin D / calcidiol), followed by 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the proximal renal tubule (stimulated by PTH)
24-hydroxylation in adipose tissue followed by carboxylation in bone
Sulfation in the stomach followed by glucuronidation in the colon
questions.explain: Hepatic 25-hydroxylase (CYP2R1) forms 25(OH)D (the main circulating storage form measured clinically), and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1, induced by PTH and inhibited by FGF23) forms active 1,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol).

open.q: Name the active hormonal form of vitamin D produced by renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D.

questions.q: How does calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) raise serum calcium and phosphate concentrations while supporting bone mineralization?
options: Directly inhibits all intestinal ion transport

Increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption (via TRPV6, calbindin-D9k, and NaPi-IIb), promotes renal calcium reabsorption, and mobilizes calcium/phosphate from bone with PTH to maintain extracellular Ca x PO4 supersaturation for osteoid mineralization
Promotes renal phosphate wasting exclusively without affecting calcium
Converts osteoid into collagenase
questions.explain: Adequate serum Ca2+ and PO4^3- supplied by calcitriol action are required to mineralize osteoid; vitamin D deficiency or severe renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase loss causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

open.q: What is the adult bone mineralization defect analogous to childhood rickets caused by vitamin D deficiency?

questions.q: Which vitamin acts primarily as a lipid-soluble peroxyl radical scavenger that terminates free-radical chain lipid peroxidation in cell membranes?
options: Vitamin K
Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol)
Vitamin B12
Vitamin B6
questions.explain: Alpha-tocopherol donates a phenolic hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO.), halting propagation of membrane lipid peroxidation; deficiency can cause hemolytic anemia, spinocerebellar ataxia, and peripheral neuropathy.

open.q: Name the most biologically active vitamer of vitamin E.

questions.q: Why do exclusively breastfed newborns routinely receive intramuscular vitamin K shortly after birth?
options: Breast milk contains high levels of warfarin

Newborns have sterile guts (lacking vitamin K2-producing intestinal bacteria), low transplacental vitamin K stores, and low vitamin K content in breast milk, putting them at risk for vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB / hemorrhagic disease of the newborn)
Vitamin K prevents physiological neonatal jaundice by blocking bilirubin production
Newborns cannot absorb water from milk
questions.explain: Vitamin K is required for gamma-glutamyl carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S; neonatal prophylaxis prevents intracranial and gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

open.q: Which four procoagulant clotting factors require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation?
accept: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

questions.q: In its active coenzyme form thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which three key dehydrogenase and transketolase enzymes depend on vitamin B1 (thiamine)?
options: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and transketolase (plus branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase)
Glycogen phosphorylase, alanine aminotransferase, and glutamate decarboxylase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase
Pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase
questions.explain: TPP stabilizes acyl/hydroxyethyl carbanion intermediates in oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids (pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, BCKDH) and in pentose phosphate pathway transketolase; deficiency causes dry/wet beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

open.q: State the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1 (thiamine).

questions.q: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus and lateral rectus palsy), and gait ataxia, and later develops severe anterograde amnesia and confabulation. Why must thiamine be administered BEFORE or concurrently with glucose infusion in such patients?
options: Glucose increases renal excretion of thiamine
Administering glucose without thiamine drives pyruvate metabolism and acute TPP consumption, precipitating or worsening fatal Wernicke encephalopathy
Glucose converts thiamine into cyanide
Thiamine blocks insulin secretion
questions.explain: In thiamine-depleted patients, a glucose load increases glycolytic pyruvate flux when pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase lack TPP, worsening cellular energy failure in vulnerable diencephalic and brainstem nuclei.

open.q: Name the classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy caused by thiamine deficiency.

questions.q: Which two redox coenzymes are derived from vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and participate in one- and two-electron transfer reactions (such as succinate dehydrogenase and acyl-CoA dehydrogenase)?
options: NAD+ and NADP+
FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide)
Coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein
Tetrahydrofolate and S-adenosylmethionine
questions.explain: Riboflavin forms FMN and FAD, whose isoalloxazine ring accepts/donates electrons; ariboflavinosis causes cheilosis (angular stomatitis), glossitis (magenta tongue), and seborrheic dermatitis/corneal vascularization.

open.q: Name the two coenzymes synthesized from vitamin B2 (riboflavin).

questions.q: Which essential amino acid serves as an endogenous precursor for niacin (NAD+/NADP+) synthesis in humans, and which clinical syndrome ('the 4 Ds': dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death) results from niacin deficiency?
options: Tyrosine; scurvy
Tryptophan; pellagra
Methionine; pernicious anemia
Histidine; rickets
questions.explain: Approximately 60 mg of dietary tryptophan yields ~1 mg of niacin equivalents (requiring vitamin B6 and B2 along the kynurenine-quinolinate pathway); pellagra occurs in maize-reliant diets (niacin is bound/unavailable in untreated corn unless nixtamalized) or in Hartnup disease and carcinoid syndrome (excessive tryptophan diversion to serotonin).

open.q: Name the deficiency disease of niacin (vitamin B3) classically characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

questions.q: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is an essential structural component of which two central metabolic acyl-carrying cofactors?
options: Biotin and lipoic acid
Pyridoxal phosphate and tetrahydrofolate
Coenzyme A (CoA) and acyl carrier protein (ACP)
Cobalamin and ubiquinone
questions.explain: Pantothenic acid provides the pantoate and beta-alanine/cysteamine (4'-phosphopantetheine) moiety of Coenzyme A (used in TCA cycle, fatty acid oxidation/synthesis, and acetylation) and fatty acid synthase's ACP.

open.q: Name the central acyl-carrying coenzyme derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5).

questions.q: In its active coenzyme form pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), which biochemical reactions depend on vitamin B6?
options: Fatty acid beta-oxidation and ketogenesis
Purine ring de novo synthesis exclusively
Transaminases (aminotransferases), decarboxylases (e.g., heme ALA synthase, neurotransmitter synthesis of GABA/serotonin/dopamine/norepinephrine/histamine), and glycogen phosphorylase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
questions.explain: PLP forms a Schiff base (aldimine) with amino substrates to facilitate transamination, alpha/beta-elimination, racemization, and decarboxylation, and also serves as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase.

open.q: State the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6.

questions.q: Which carboxylase enzymes require biotin (vitamin B7) as a covalently bound CO2 carrier?
options: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Transketolase and transaldolase
Methionine synthase and thymidylate synthase
Pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and propionyl-CoA carboxylase
questions.explain: Biotin carries activated carboxyl groups (-COO-) via ATP-dependent carboxylation of its ureido ring; chronic consumption of raw egg whites contains avidin, which binds biotin tightly and can cause dermatitis, alopecia, and enteritis.

open.q: Name the tetrameric protein in raw egg whites that binds biotin with very high affinity and prevents its absorption.

questions.q: How does folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anemia without causing the subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord seen in vitamin B12 deficiency?
options: Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis; B12 deficiency also disrupts myelin maintenance through methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
Folate deficiency selectively blocks haem synthesis, whereas B12 deficiency blocks iron absorption
Folate is stored in the liver for years, whereas B12 is rapidly excreted
Only folate is needed for red-cell maturation; B12 is needed only for nerve conduction
questions.explain: Both folate and B12 deficiencies impair thymidylate synthesis and cause megaloblastic anemia ('methyl trap' in B12 deficiency traps folate as N5-methyl-THF), while only B12 deficiency impairs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (accumulating methylmalonic acid) and causes demyelination.

open.q: Which enzyme converts homocysteine to methionine using N5-methyltetrahydrofolate and methylcobalamin (vitamin B12)?

questions.q: Why is periconceptional folic acid supplementation recommended before and during early pregnancy?
options: Prevents gestational diabetes mellitus
Reduces the risk of neural tube defects (such as spina bifida and anencephaly) by supporting rapid nucleotide synthesis and one-carbon methylation during neural tube closure
Increases maternal red blood cell lifespan to 200 days
Replaces dietary calcium intake
questions.explain: Neural tube closure occurs within the first ~28 days post-conception—often before a pregnancy is recognized—making adequate folate status prior to conception critical for DNA synthesis and neural tube closure.

open.q: Periconceptional folic acid supplementation primarily reduces the risk of which group of congenital malformations?

questions.q: Which gastric glycoprotein is required in the distal ileum for receptor-mediated absorption of dietary vitamin B12 (cobalamin), and what condition results from autoimmune destruction of parietal cells or intrinsic factor?
options: Haptocorrin (R-protein); Gilbert syndrome
Transcobalamin II; Wilson disease
Intrinsic factor (Castle's intrinsic factor); pernicious anemia
Albumin; hemochromatosis
questions.explain: Salivary haptocorrin binds B12 in the stomach; pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin in the duodenum so B12 can bind gastric intrinsic factor, which is then absorbed via cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum and transported in blood by transcobalamin II.

open.q: Name the gastric glycoprotein essential for intestinal absorption of vitamin B12 whose autoimmune loss causes pernicious anemia.

questions.q: Which post-translational hydroxylation reaction requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as an electron donor to maintain iron in its reduced ferrous (Fe2+) state inside dioxygenase enzymes?
options: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate
Biotinylation of lysine
Methylation of cytosine
Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen (via prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases) to stabilize the collagen triple helix
questions.explain: Hydroxyproline forms stabilizing interchain hydrogen bonds in the collagen triple helix, and hydroxylysine provides sites for glycosylation and cross-linking; scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) causes defective collagen, fragile capillaries, bleeding gums, petechiae, perifollicular hemorrhage, and poor wound healing.

open.q: Name the deficiency disease of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) caused by impaired collagen hydroxylation.

questions.q: How does vitamin C enhance non-heme iron absorption from plant foods in the small intestine?
options: Reduces ferric iron (Fe3+) to more soluble ferrous iron (Fe2+) in the gut lumen and forms a soluble chelate complex that resists precipitation at higher duodenal pH
Binds iron to intrinsic factor in the stomach
Converts heme iron into transferrin inside enterocytes
Inhibits hepcidin synthesis permanently
questions.explain: Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) on enterocytes transports Fe2+; reducing dietary Fe3+ to Fe2+ and chelating it keeps iron soluble for absorption, whereas phytates, tannins/polyphenols, oxalates, and excess calcium inhibit non-heme iron absorption.

open.q: Which iron oxidation state (Fe2+ or Fe3+) is transported across the apical enterocyte membrane by DMT1?

questions.q: How does parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulate serum calcium and phosphate levels across bone, kidney, and indirectly the intestine?
options: Lowers serum calcium and raises phosphate by inhibiting osteoclast activity
Raises serum calcium and lowers phosphate through effects on bone and kidney; it also stimulates calcitriol production
Raises both calcium and phosphate by increasing their renal reabsorption
Lowers both calcium and phosphate by suppressing intestinal absorption
questions.explain: PTH acts rapidly on bone and kidney to raise serum Ca2+ and lower serum PO4^3-, while inducing renal CYP27B1 to boost calcitriol for sustained intestinal calcium uptake.

open.q: Which peptide hormone increases renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, promotes renal calcium reabsorption, and reduces renal phosphate reabsorption?

questions.q: How does calcitonin (secreted by parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland in response to hypercalcemia) oppose parathyroid hormone?
options: Stimulates osteoclast bone resorption
Inhibits osteoclast activity and bone resorption to lower serum calcium
Increases intestinal calcium absorption
Stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase
questions.explain: Calcitonin acts directly on osteoclast calcitonin receptors to reduce bone resorption and lower serum calcium (though its physiological role in adult human calcium homeostasis is modest compared with PTH and vitamin D).

open.q: Which cell type in the thyroid gland secretes calcitonin?

questions.q: How does FGF23 (fibroblast growth factor 23), secreted mainly by osteocytes and osteoblasts, regulate phosphate and vitamin D metabolism?
options: Increases renal phosphate reabsorption and stimulates calcitriol

Acts as a phosphaturic hormone by downregulating renal proximal sodium-phosphate cotransporters (NaPi-IIa/NaPi-IIc) to increase urinary phosphate excretion and inhibiting renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase while inducing 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) to lower calcitriol
Stimulates PTH secretion from parathyroid chief cells
Increases intestinal phosphate absorption
questions.explain: Excess FGF23 (as in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets or tumor-induced osteomalacia) causes renal phosphate wasting and inappropriately low calcitriol, resulting in hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia.

open.q: State the acronym for fibroblast growth factor 23, a key bone-derived phosphaturic hormone that lowers serum phosphate and calcitriol.

questions.q: Why is magnesium (Mg2+) essential as a cofactor for ATP-utilizing enzymes and parathyroid hormone function?
options: Mg2+ coordinates with phosphate groups of ATP (forming biologically active Mg-ATP2-) in kinases and ATPases, and severe hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and target-organ responsiveness ('functional hypoparathyroidism')
Mg2+ replaces hemoglobin iron in red blood cells
Mg2+ is the primary extracellular anion
Mg2+ prevents all neuromuscular excitability
questions.explain: Most kinases, synthetases, and ATPases recognize the Mg-ATP complex as their true substrate; severe magnesium depletion blunts PTH release and causes refractory hypocalcemia until magnesium is repleted.

open.q: With which nucleotide triphosphate does Mg2+ form the biologically active substrate complex required by most kinases and synthetases?

questions.q: How do aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH / vasopressin) regulate sodium, potassium, and water balance differently?
options: Aldosterone increases renal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion; ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability
Aldosterone increases free-water excretion; ADH increases potassium secretion
Both hormones act mainly in the proximal tubule to increase glucose reabsorption
ADH increases sodium excretion, whereas aldosterone inhibits water reabsorption
questions.explain: Aldosterone (a mineralocorticoid) upregulates ENaC, Na+/K+-ATPase, and H+-ATPase/ROMK in collecting duct principal/intercalated cells, whereas ADH (vasopressin) promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells.

open.q: Which water channel protein is inserted into the apical membrane of renal collecting duct principal cells in response to antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: How does hepcidin (a peptide hormone synthesized primarily by the liver) regulate systemic iron homeostasis?
options: Activates ferroportin to increase iron release into plasma
Binds ferroportin and promotes its degradation, reducing intestinal iron absorption and macrophage iron release
Increases transferrin synthesis to deliver more iron to marrow
Converts ferric iron into ferrous iron within circulating erythrocytes
questions.explain: Hepcidin rises with high iron stores or inflammation (via IL-6), degrading ferroportin to limit iron entry into plasma; conversely, hepcidin deficiency (e.g., HFE mutation) causes excessive iron absorption and hereditary hemochromatosis.

open.q: Name the hepatic peptide hormone that degrades ferroportin to inhibit iron export into plasma.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: Which plasma glycoprotein transports ferric iron (Fe3+) in circulation, and which cytosolic protein stores iron safely inside cells?
options: Ceruloplasmin; hemosiderin
Transferrin; ferritin
Albumin; myoglobin
Haptoglobin; cytochrome c
questions.explain: Transferrin binds two Fe3+ ions in plasma and delivers them via transferrin receptor-mediated endocytosis; ferritin is a multimeric iron-storage shell (up to ~4,500 Fe3+ atoms), while hemosiderin represents degraded insoluble ferritin aggregates in iron overload.

open.q: Name the main iron-transporting protein in blood plasma.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: A 46-year-old man presents with fatigue, arthralgias, bronze skin pigmentation, hepatomegaly, elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (>45%), and diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes'). Why does excess iron cause multiorgan damage?
options: Iron catalyzes Fenton and Haber-Weiss reactions to generate highly reactive hydroxyl radicals (.OH) that cause lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, and tissue fibrosis in liver, pancreas, heart, joints, and pituitary
Iron directly inhibits insulin receptors without radical formation
Iron depletes all dietary vitamins
Excess iron causes acute hypokalemia
questions.explain: Free redox-active iron catalyzes Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> Fe3+ + .OH + OH-), driving oxidative injury and fibrosis (cirrhosis, restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy, diabetes, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism); treated with therapeutic phlebotomy or iron chelators (deferoxamine, deferasirox).

open.q: Name the iron-catalyzed chemical reaction that generates toxic hydroxyl radicals from hydrogen peroxide.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: How does copper participate in iron metabolism and connective tissue crosslinking?
options: Copper is required for ferroxidase activity of ceruloplasmin (and hephaestin) to oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ for transferrin loading, and for lysyl oxidase to crosslink collagen and elastin
Copper replaces magnesium in ATP
Copper is a component of vitamin B12
Copper inhibits cytochrome c oxidase
questions.explain: Ceruloplasmin is the major copper-carrying plasma protein and acts as a ferroxidase required for iron mobilization/transferrin binding; copper is also a cofactor for cytochrome c oxidase and superoxide dismutase.

open.q: Name the copper-containing plasma ferroxidase protein whose deficiency or dysfunction is characteristic of Wilson disease and aceruloplasminemia.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with neuropsychiatric symptoms (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, behavioral changes), elevated liver enzymes, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam, and low serum ceruloplasmin with increased 24-hour urinary copper excretion. Mutation in which copper-transporting P-type ATPase causes Wilson disease?
options: ATP7A
ATP7B
HFE
SLC40A1
questions.explain: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive mutation in ATP7B (hepatocyte copper exporter into bile and ceruloplasmin), leading to copper accumulation in liver, basal ganglia, and Descemet membrane of the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings); Menkes disease results from X-linked ATP7A mutations causing defective intestinal copper export and kinky hair/neurodegeneration.

open.q: Which copper-transporting ATPase gene is mutated in Wilson disease?

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: Which clinical features are characteristic of zinc deficiency in humans?
options: Acrodermatitis enteropathica (periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea), impaired wound healing, hypogonadism/growth retardation, and dysgeusia (altered taste)/anosmia
Macrocytic megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration
Hemarthroses and prolonged aPTT
Chocolate-brown blood and methemoglobinemia
questions.explain: Zinc is a structural and catalytic cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors (including zinc fingers, alkaline phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase, alcohol dehydrogenase, and Cu/Zn-SOD); phytates in unrefined cereal diets reduce zinc bioavailability.

open.q: Name the inherited or acquired zinc-deficiency disorder characterized by periorificial/acral rash, alopecia, and diarrhea.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: Which trace element is an essential structural component of thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4, containing four iodine atoms) and triiodothyronine (T3, containing three iodine atoms)?
options: Fluorine
Iodine
Manganese
Chromium
questions.explain: Thyroid follicular cells trap iodide (I-) via the basolateral Na+/I- symporter (NIS), oxidize it via thyroperoxidase (TPO), and iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to form MIT and DIT, which couple into T3 and T4; dietary iodine deficiency causes endemic goiter and hypothyroidism.

open.q: How many iodine atoms are present in a molecule of thyroxine (T4)?

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: Which trace element is incorporated as selenocysteine into selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidase and iodothyronine deiodinases (which convert T4 to active T3)?
options: Selenium
Cobalt
Molybdenum
Nickel
questions.explain: Selenium is encoded via the UGA stop codon in selenoprotein mRNAs using a specific tRNA^[Ser]Sec; severe deficiency (especially with coxsackievirus) is associated with Keshan cardiomyopathy and Kashin-Beck osteoarthropathy.

open.q: Which 21st amino acid incorporates selenium into glutathione peroxidase and iodothyronine deiodinases?

questions.sub: Nutrition in Special States and Refeeding Syndrome
questions.q: Why does refeeding syndrome occur when malnourished or prolonged-fasting patients are rapidly fed high-carbohydrate calories without adequate electrolyte and vitamin supplementation?
options: Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, causing potentially dangerous serum depletion
Rapid feeding causes immediate hypercalcaemia and sodium retention
Refeeding suppresses insulin and causes severe hyperglycaemia
High-carbohydrate feeding prevents cellular ATP synthesis
questions.explain: During starvation, intracellular phosphate, potassium, and magnesium stores are depleted despite near-normal serum levels; refeeding insulin shifts these ions into cells and consumes phosphate/thiamine in anabolic phosphorylation, requiring slow caloric advancement, electrolyte repletion, and thiamine supplementation.

open.q: Which hallmark electrolyte abnormality in refeeding syndrome can cause cardiac arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, and diaphragmatic/respiratory failure?

questions.sub: Nutrition in Special States and Refeeding Syndrome
questions.q: What is the biochemical basis of lactose intolerance in adults with lactase non-persistence?
options: Low brush-border lactase leaves lactose unabsorbed, causing osmotic diarrhoea and bacterial fermentation
IgE-mediated allergy to milk proteins causes immediate mast-cell degranulation
Excess hepatic galactose production overwhelms renal excretion
Failure of intestinal glucose transport prevents lactose digestion
questions.explain: Primary adult-type hypolactasia (lactase non-persistence) is the most common cause of lactose intolerance worldwide; unabsorbed osmotically active disaccharide increases luminal water and undergoes bacterial fermentation.

open.q: Name the brush-border disaccharidase enzyme deficient in lactose intolerance.

questions.q: Which two polyunsaturated fatty acids are nutritionally essential in humans because mammalian desaturases cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon-9 (omega-9) counting from the methyl (omega) end?
options: Linoleic acid (18:2, omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (18:3, omega-3)
Palmitic acid (16:0) and stearic acid (18:0)
Oleic acid (18:1, omega-9) and butyric acid (4:0)
Arachidic acid (20:0) and lignoceric acid (24:0)
questions.explain: Humans lack delta-12 and delta-15 desaturases needed to synthesize omega-6 (linoleic acid) and omega-3 (alpha-linolenic acid) fatty acids de novo; linoleic acid serves as precursor for arachidonic acid (eicosanoids) and alpha-linolenic acid for EPA and DHA.

open.q: Name the two essential fatty acids required in the human diet.

questions.q: How do trans unsaturated fatty acids adversely affect plasma lipid profiles and cardiovascular risk compared with cis unsaturated fatty acids?
options: Trans fatty acids have a straighter conformation that packs more tightly, raising LDL cholesterol and lipoprotein(a) while lowering HDL cholesterol and promoting endothelial inflammation/atherosclerosis
Trans fatty acids lower LDL cholesterol and raise HDL cholesterol
Trans fatty acids cannot be absorbed by enterocytes
Trans fatty acids convert into essential omega-3 fatty acids
questions.explain: Partially hydrogenated vegetable oils produce trans double bonds with higher melting points and adverse lipoprotein effects (raising LDL, lowering HDL), prompting global public health elimination of industrial trans fats.

open.q: Do trans fatty acids generally increase or decrease LDL cholesterol levels in human plasma?

questions.q: What is the glycemic index (GI) of a carbohydrate-containing food, and how does it differ from glycemic load (GL)?
options: Glycemic index measures how quickly and high a standardized 50-g available carbohydrate portion raises blood glucose relative to glucose or white bread, whereas glycemic load multiplies GI by the actual grams of available carbohydrate in a typical serving
Glycemic index measures total calorie density; glycemic load measures fiber content
Both terms refer exclusively to dietary protein
Glycemic index is always equal to zero for fruit
questions.explain: Glycemic load accounts for both carbohydrate quality (GI) and serving portion size (GL = [GI x grams of available carb] / 100), providing a more practical measure of postprandial glycemic impact.

open.q: Which metric incorporates both a food's glycemic index and the actual portion size of carbohydrate consumed?

questions.q: What is the thermic effect of food (specific dynamic action), and which macronutrient typically elicits the highest thermic effect?
options: The energy expended in digesting, absorbing, transporting, and metabolizing nutrients; protein (~20-30% of its energy) has a higher thermic effect than carbohydrate (~5-10%) or fat (~0-3%)
Heat generated strictly by shivering in cold weather
Calories lost in feces due to constipation
Energy spent chewing gum
questions.explain: Amino acid deamination, urea synthesis, and peptide bond formation require substantial ATP expenditure, giving dietary protein a higher thermic effect than carbohydrates or fats.

open.q: Which macronutrient (carbohydrate, protein, or fat) has the highest thermic effect of food per kilocalorie ingested?

questions.q: How does leptin (secreted primarily by white adipose tissue in proportion to fat mass) regulate energy balance centrally?
options: Acts on hypothalamic arcuate nucleus neurons to stimulate anorexigenic POMC/CART neurons (decreasing food intake and increasing energy expenditure) and inhibit orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons
Directly stimulates gastric ghrelin release to induce hunger
Inhibits brown adipose tissue thermogenesis
Lowers insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Leptin signals adipose energy sufficiency to the hypothalamus; congenital leptin or leptin receptor deficiency causes severe hyperphagia and early-onset obesity, whereas common obesity often involves central leptin resistance despite high circulating leptin.

open.q: Name the adipose-derived satiety hormone that acts on the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure.

questions.q: How does ghrelin (an acylated peptide hormone produced mainly by gastric oxyntic/P/D1 cells before meals) affect appetite and metabolism?
options: Rises before meals to stimulate hunger via hypothalamic NPY/AgRP neurons and promotes growth hormone release, then falls after eating
Acts as a long-term satiety signal produced by adipocytes
Inhibits gastric motility and growth hormone secretion
Is secreted exclusively by the pancreas in response to hyperglycemia
questions.explain: Ghrelin is an orexigenic ('hunger') hormone whose plasma levels peak during fasting/before meals and drop postprandially.

open.q: Name the stomach-derived hormone whose levels typically rise during fasting before meals to stimulate hunger.

questions.q: Why does combined deficiency of vitamin E and selenium exacerbate oxidative tissue injury?
options: Vitamin E scavenges lipid peroxyl radicals inside membranes while selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides in the cytosol/mitochondria, providing complementary antioxidant protection
Both vitamins are required to synthesize fibrinogen
Selenium converts vitamin E into vitamin D
Vitamin E requires selenium to bind opsin
questions.explain: Working in tandem, alpha-tocopherol interrupts radical chains in lipid bilayers and glutathione peroxidase detoxifies peroxides, lowering the burden of reactive oxygen species on cellular membranes.

open.q: Which antioxidant enzyme depends on selenium to reduce hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides using glutathione?

questions.q: How do fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) depend on normal hepatobiliary and pancreatic function for intestinal absorption?
options: They dissolve in gastric acid and diffuse directly into portal blood without micelles
They are hydrophobic and require bile salts and pancreatic lipase to be incorporated into mixed micelles for enterocyte uptake and chylomicron transport into lymphatics
They are absorbed in the colon by passive osmosis alone
They bind to intrinsic factor in the stomach
questions.explain: Cholestatic liver disease, biliary obstruction, cystic fibrosis, or chronic pancreatitis impairs micelle formation or lipid digestion, causing malabsorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K and steatorrhea.

open.q: Through which lymphatic lipoprotein particles are absorbed fat-soluble vitamins and dietary triacylglycerols initially exported from enterocytes?

questions.q: Which water-soluble vitamin is stored in substantial hepatic reserves (sufficient for roughly 2 to 4+ years in healthy adults due to enterohepatic circulation and high-affinity transcobalamin/storage), unlike most other water-soluble vitamins?
options: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
Vitamin B1 (thiamine)
Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)
questions.explain: Most water-soluble vitamins are rapidly cleared in urine with modest stores (weeks to a few months), whereas vitamin B12 has large hepatic stores (~2-5 mg) and undergoes enterohepatic recycling, meaning dietary deficiency often takes years to manifest unless absorption (intrinsic factor/ileum) is impaired.

open.q: Which water-soluble vitamin typically has the largest body stores (often lasting years after dietary intake stops)?

questions.q: Which metabolic reaction is uniquely impaired in vitamin B12 deficiency (alongside methionine synthase) and leads to accumulation of methylmalonic acid in blood and urine?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (converting L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA using adenosylcobalamin)
HMG-CoA reductase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
questions.explain: Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for mitochondrial methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid catabolism; its impairment elevates methylmalonic acid (MMA) in B12 deficiency, whereas MMA is normal in isolated folate deficiency.

open.q: Which metabolite accumulates in plasma and urine in vitamin B12 deficiency but remains normal in isolated folate deficiency?

questions.q: Which coenzyme form of tetrahydrofolate (THF) donates a one-carbon methyl group to dUMP to synthesize dTMP (thymidylate) for DNA synthesis?
options: N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate (with thymidylate synthase)
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate exclusively
Vitamin K hydroquinone
Pyridoxal phosphate
questions.explain: Thymidylate synthase uses N5,N10-methylene-THF as both a one-carbon donor and reducing agent (converting THF to dihydrofolate, which dihydrofolate reductase reduces back to THF) to methylate dUMP into dTMP; methotrexate and 5-fluorouracil target this pathway.

open.q: Name the enzyme that converts dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate.

questions.q: In the treatment of severe folate deficiency, why must vitamin B12 deficiency be ruled out or treated before giving high-dose folic acid alone?
options: Folic acid can partially correct the megaloblastic anemia of B12 deficiency while allowing B12-deficient neurological demyelination (subacute combined degeneration) to progress unchecked
Folic acid precipitates calcium oxalate stones
Folic acid destroys intrinsic factor
Folic acid causes severe hypoglycemia
questions.explain: High-dose folate supplies tetrahydrofolate intermediates bypassing the B12 methyl trap for DNA synthesis/hematopoiesis, masking anemia while leaving methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and myelin maintenance impaired.

open.q: Which spinal cord and peripheral nerve disorder can progress if vitamin B12 deficiency is masked by folic acid supplementation alone?
accept: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

questions.q: How does nicotinic acid (niacin at pharmacological doses, typically grams/day) alter plasma lipoproteins?
options: Reduces adipose lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production, lowering triglycerides and LDL while raising HDL
Blocks intestinal NPC1L1 and prevents dietary cholesterol absorption
Directly activates lipoprotein lipase to clear chylomicrons
Increases hepatic cholesterol synthesis and suppresses HDL formation
questions.explain: Pharmacological niacin acts via adipocyte HCAR2/GPR109A receptors to suppress lipolysis and lowers hepatic VLDL assembly, raising HDL and lowering LDL/triglycerides.

open.q: Which vitamin (at high pharmacological doses) lowers LDL and triglycerides while raising HDL, but commonly causes cutaneous flushing?

questions.q: Why does chronic kidney disease (CKD) with reduced glomerular filtration rate frequently lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy?
options: Phosphate retention raises serum phosphate (stimulating FGF23 and binding Ca2+) while impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase lowers calcitriol (reducing intestinal Ca2+ absorption), causing hypocalcemia that chronically stimulates PTH secretion
Kidneys secrete excess thyroxine in CKD
CKD increases intestinal calcium absorption ten-fold
CKD lowers serum phosphate to zero
questions.explain: Reduced phosphate clearance, hyperphosphatemia, falling calcitriol, and hypocalcemia drive continuous parathyroid chief-cell hyperplasia and PTH hypersecretion in chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD).

open.q: In chronic kidney disease, reduced activity of which renal enzyme contributes to low calcitriol and hypocalcemia?

questions.q: Which clinical signs of neuromuscular excitability (hypocalcemic tetany) appear when ionized serum calcium falls markedly?
options: Carpopedal spasm, muscle cramps/twitching, circumoral paresthesia, Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, and prolonged QT interval on ECG
Generalized flaccid paralysis and shortened QT interval
Loss of deep tendon reflexes with hypercalcemic stupor
Absence of all action potentials
questions.explain: Low extracellular Ca2+ reduces screening of negative charges on voltage-gated Na+ channels, causing them to open at less negative membrane potentials and increasing neuronal/muscular excitability.

open.q: Name one classic clinical sign of hypocalcemic neuromuscular excitability elicited on physical examination.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: How do phytates (inositol hexakisphosphate) in unfermented whole grains, legumes, and seeds affect mineral nutrition?
options: Chelate divalent cations (such as zinc, iron, and calcium) in the intestinal lumen into insoluble complexes that reduce their absorption, which can be partially reduced by soaking, sprouting, or fermentation (phytase activity)
Increase vitamin D synthesis in the skin
Convert dietary protein into essential fatty acids
Eliminate the need for dietary iron
questions.explain: Phytic acid binds positively charged metal ions (Zn2+, Fe2+, Ca2+, Mg2+), lowering mineral bioavailability unless degraded by food processing (fermentation, sourdough leavening, germination) or endogenous/dietary phytases.

open.q: Name the phosphorus-storage compound in plant grains and legumes that binds divalent minerals like zinc and iron and reduces their absorption.

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: What is the biochemical difference between iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation)?
options: Iron deficiency has low serum ferritin (<30 ng/mL) and high total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), whereas anemia of inflammation has elevated hepcidin trapping iron in macrophages/reticuloendothelial stores, resulting in normal-to-high serum ferritin, low serum iron, and low/normal TIBC
Anemia of inflammation has high TIBC and very low ferritin
Iron deficiency has high serum ferritin and high hepcidin
Both anemias are caused by vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.explain: Inflammatory cytokines (especially IL-6) upregulate hepatic hepcidin, blocking ferroportin export and raising ferritin (an acute-phase reactant), whereas true iron depletion lowers ferritin and increases hepatic transferrin (TIBC) synthesis.

open.q: How does total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) typically behave in iron deficiency anemia versus anemia of chronic inflammation?
accept: High in iron deficiency and low or normal in anemia of inflammation
Increased in iron deficiency, decreased in chronic inflammation

questions.sub: Iron, Copper, Zinc, and Iodine Metabolism
questions.q: Why does chronic antacid or proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy or prior gastrectomy impair non-heme iron and vitamin B12 absorption?
options: Reduced gastric acid (hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria) impairs solubilization and Fe3+ release from food and reduces acid/pepsin-mediated cleavage of food-bound vitamin B12 from dietary proteins
Gastric acid is needed to synthesize vitamin D
Antacids convert ferritin into hemoglobin
Gastric acid absorbs all dietary potassium
questions.explain: Stomach acid helps solubilize dietary iron and cleaves dietary proteins to release vitamin B12 for transfer to haptocorrin and subsequently intrinsic factor.

open.q: How does chronic reduction of gastric acid secretion (e.g., from PPIs or achlorhydria) affect food-bound vitamin B12 absorption?
accept: Impairs release of vitamin B12 from food proteins

questions.sub: Nutrition in Special States and Refeeding Syndrome
questions.q: Why do pregnant and lactating individuals have elevated requirements for iron, folate, calcium, and protein?
options: To support expanded maternal blood volume and red cell mass, fetal/placental tissue growth and fetal iron/calcium accretion, and milk synthesis (lactose, casein/whey proteins, and calcium)
Because metabolic rate drops to zero during pregnancy
Because the kidneys stop filtering nutrients during lactation
Only to replace sweat losses
questions.explain: Maternal erythropoiesis expansion, fetal/placental growth, and human milk production (~700-800 mL/day in established lactation) substantially increase demands for energy, protein, iron, folate, iodine, and micronutrients.

open.q: Which two micronutrients are especially critical during pregnancy to support maternal red cell expansion, fetal growth, and neural tube development?

questions.q: What is basal metabolic rate (BMR) / resting energy expenditure (REE), and which organ contributes the largest share of resting energy expenditure per kilogram of tissue?
options: Energy expended at rest in a thermoneutral, post-absorptive state to maintain vital organ/cellular functions; brain, liver, heart, and kidneys have very high metabolic rates per unit mass (while skeletal muscle is large in total mass)
Energy expended during maximum sprinting
Energy lost exclusively through urine
Energy consumed by sleeping less than 4 hours
questions.explain: Basal/resting metabolic rate accounts for roughly 60-75% of total daily energy expenditure in sedentary individuals and is influenced by lean body mass, age, sex, thyroid hormone status, and body surface area/temperature.

open.q: Approximately what percentage of total daily energy expenditure does resting/basal metabolic rate typically represent in a sedentary adult?
